articles.title: The moment I knew: He quoted my favourite TV show. I blurted out, ‘Marry me!’
articles.summary: On Anthony Ashdown’s first date with Jake, their mutual love of nerd culture felt revolutionary. Then Jake referenced a catchphrase from The Golden Girls. Find more stories from the moment I knew series. Picture it. Sydney. 2015. I had weathered a nasty breakup the previous year.
body: I got on the apps and matched with Jake, a handsome young man 10 years younger than me. We chatted on Grindr and planned to meet for coffee and then spend the afternoon at Cronulla beach.

Days later, on a hot summer morning, I sat waiting in a coffee shop at Miranda Fair. My heart was thumping. This was the first date I’d been on since the breakup. Sure, there’d been plenty of hookups. What gay doesn’t go through his footloose and fancy-free phase post heartbreak? But this was the first real date. And at 33, for some reason, I felt old. What did this cute young thing see in me, that he reached out to me?
He arrived soon after. We’d already covered some ground when chatting online, so the ice breakers and awkwardness were out of the way already.

I laid all my cards on the table. I had nothing to lose. I was about to become a surrogate father with a lesbian couple. I intended on being a part of this child’s life and I wasn’t going to accept anyone in my romantic life who took issue with that, or didn’t want to be a part of that themselves. He wasn’t fazed in the slightest by it.
points: On Anthony Ashdown’s first date with Jake, their mutual love of nerd culture felt revolutionary.

articles.title: All Accounted for After Tanker Crashes Into Docked New Orleans Riverboat
articles.summary: Gov. Jeff Landry of Louisiana called it a “literal miracle on the Mississippi” that all of the nearly 200 people aboard the riverboat were rescued.
body: A tanker ship struck a riverboat carrying nearly 200 people on Friday in New Orleans, causing the cruise ship to capsize at its dock and prompting a wide-scale search-and-rescue operation, the authorities said.
Mayor Helena Moreno of New Orleans said at a news conference that all passengers of the riverboat, the American Heritage, were accounted for after the crash.
A city of New Orleans spokesperson said on Friday that 32 people were hospitalized. On Saturday the city’s deputy mayor of health and human services said two people had serious injuries.
“It is a literal miracle on the Mississippi,” said Gov. Jeff Landry of Louisiana, who also spoke at the news conference.
points: Jeff Landry of Louisiana called it a “literal miracle on the Mississippi” that all of the nearly 200 people aboard the riverboat were rescued.

articles.title: How Some Flights Were Exempt From the Ground Stop
articles.summary: Dozens of international flights departed from the United States during Friday’s nationwide ground stop. Some planes also left for Hawaii from the West Coast.
body: Thousands of passengers scrambled to update their travel plans on Saturday as air traffic slowly unsnarled after a nationwide ground stop on Friday, but a number of travelers had already arrived at their destinations on flights left unaffected by the order.

Dozens of international flights took to the skies even as airports across the United States coped with only the third nationwide ground stop issued by the Federal Aviation Administration this century. Certain flights were also permitted to depart from the West Coast to Hawaii during the stoppage.
Here’s why some air travel was allowed to proceed even as flight systems were hampered.
More than 8,200 flights were canceled nationwide on Friday — over 31 percent of those scheduled — according to Cirium, an aviation data firm.
points: Dozens of international flights departed from the United States during Friday’s nationwide ground stop.

articles.title: ‘You have to cope’: why don’t we hear of the ‘epidemic’ of women’s loneliness?
articles.summary: The world has become accustomed to concerns about the male loneliness epidemic. But research suggests women are just as lonely. Sign up for a weekly email featuring our best reads. No one would think of Sasha* as lonely, least of all Sasha herself.
body: “All those things that you read about, about why men might be lonely – they don’t maintain one-on-one friendships, or they’re not good at reaching out, or their conversations aren’t deep and meaningful – none of those issues apply to me,” she says. “I’m a very socially connected person.”

Yet Sasha often felt lonely during her first year of motherhood, even when she was surrounded by other people. (All case studies’ names have been changed.) She attributes it now to the intensity of the experience. “It’s the identity shift of your first child, having no idea of what you’re doing, learning on the fly … You feel alone.”

We’re living through a global crisis of loneliness, with the World Health Organization (WHO) declaring it a priority for public health, but it’s hard to miss that the coverage and conversation has been overwhelmingly focused on men.
Global Google searches for “male loneliness” spiked suddenly in mid-2023, and have since seen frequent surges; interest in “female loneliness”, meanwhile, has remained a trickle.

articles.title: E.T., Phone Chanel! How Fashion’s Labels Got Personal Again
articles.summary: From Steven Spielberg’s secret Chanel embroidery to love letters, playful logos, and little lambs, fashion is finding new ways to wear its heart on its sleeve—or, rather, inside its lining.
body: E.T., phone home! Or if you’re Steven Spielberg g etting honored at the Museum of Modern Art’s annual Film Benefit, phone Chanel. On Thursday night, Spielberg offered a peek inside his bespoke Chanel tuxedo jacket, courtesy of Matthieu Blazy. Beneath the classic black tailoring was a galaxy-speckled lining, an embroidered playing card featuring E.T. on his bicycle, and a little patch reading “E.T. PHONE HOME.” Spielberg proudly flashed the details for all to see. Now that’s a statement lining.

It’s just the latest in a series of delightfully personal flourishes coming out of Blazy’s Chanel atelier. For his spring 2026 haute couture debut, the designer asked models to contribute something meaningful to their looks: a love letter, a birth date, a lucky symbol, an intimate thought. These were translated into exquisite embroideries by the house’s Lesage atelier, stitched into garments or onto little silk notes tucked inside delicate, translucent Chanel handbags. Model Stephanie Cavalli reportedly chose a letter from her husband. The sentiment was just as beautiful as the craftsmanship.
points: From Steven Spielberg’s secret Chanel embroidery to love letters, playful logos, and little lambs, fashion is finding new ways to wear its heart on its sleeve—or, rather, inside its lining.

articles.title: They Spent Millions to Keep Their Dream Cruise Afloat. It Died Anyway.
articles.summary: Secrecy, debt and soaring fuel costs all contributed to the Odyssey’s downfall. Here’s an inside look at how the “endless cruise” unraveled.
body: That’s what Benjamin Schatz, a Harvard-educated lawyer, says he told his friends two years ago when he invested more than $500,000 to buy cabins and equity in Villa Vie Residences, a start-up offering a multiyear residential cruise.

Last week, its cruise ship, called the Odyssey, ground to a sudden halt in Cambodia when the ship’s operators announced that they could no longer afford fuel. Given hours to disembark, the Odyssey’s 200 passengers, some of whom had sold their homes and used their retirement savings to live on the ship, found themselves stranded in Southeast Asia. On Wednesday, Villa Vie’s main lender took control of the ship, which was still laden with passenger belongings. The Odyssey is now headed to Singapore, where it may be auctioned off.
But Mr. Schatz, 67, a former adviser to President Bill Clinton, isn’t ready to call himself a fool. “It was a glorious experience,” he said, “and one that I’m not prepared to end.”

articles.title: Why Foraging for Food Is the Latest Trend in Luxury Hotels and Fine-Dining Restaurants
articles.summary: The latest trend at country hotels and fine-dining restaurants, these excursions are designed to bring out the hunter-gatherer instinct in their guests.
body: IT’S BEEN MORE than 20 years since the Danish chefs Claus Meyer, René Redzepi and Mads Refslund sailed through sea caves in the Faroe Islands and explored geysers in Iceland in search of culinary inspiration found in natural habitats. Many of their discoveries — sea buckthorn berries that taste like tart oranges, citrusy wild thyme and intensely flavorful seaweed — made their way onto the menu at Noma, which opened in 2003 in Copenhagen and spurred the New Nordic food movement, granting the figure of the chef-forager a kind of exalted status.
points: The latest trend at country hotels and fine-dining restaurants, these excursions are designed to bring out the hunter-gatherer instinct in their guests.

articles.summary: Daily Americanos can't help with a stubborn cold, but takeout sushi and a Little Caesars Chicago Deep Dish Meat Treat pizza are good for the soul.
body: Welcome to The Receipt, a series documenting how Bon Appétit readers eat and what they spend doing it. Each food diary follows one anonymous reader’s week of expenses related to groceries, restaurant meals, coffee runs, and every bite in between. In this time of rising food costs, The Receipt reveals how folks—from different cities, with different incomes, on different schedules—are figuring out their food budgets.
In today's Receipt, we follow a 43-year-old server and drag queen in Toronto, Ontario. Keep reading for his receipts.

What is your annual salary, if you have one? Girl, I have no idea. Waiting tables brings in around $60K CAN, and performing in bars, nightclubs and drag brunches probably makes me another $3K, but all those sweat and glitter covered bills get stuffed under a mattress, so who knows?
How much is one paycheck, after taxes? Let’s call it an even thousand dollars.

articles.title: What’s My Lebensphilosophie? I Went to the Austrian Alps to Find Out
articles.summary: Writer Bridget Knowles seeks out the Austrian philosophy behind Hotel Nesslerhof, an alpine wellness resort in Austria’s Großarl Valley that encourages guests to get in the buff.
body: When I was told the general rule of thumb at Hotel Nesslerhof, an alpine wellness resort nestled in Austria’s Großar l Valley, was that it’s weird if you’re not naked, I listened.

In Austria, being naked isn’t just a physical state. It’s an emotional state, too. Austrians strip themselves down, both figuratively and literally, to achieve a mindset they call “Lebensgefühl,” a deep mind-body awareness and lifestyle that is difficult to define, let alone translate.
Großar l Valley, also known as the “Valley of Alpine Pastures" in the Salzburger Land region of Austria.

Originally a German concept, the idea stems from “Lebensphilosophie,” a 19th-century intellectual movement popularized by big name thinkers like Friedrich Nietzsche, Georg Simmel, and Wilhelm Dilthey. Translating to “philosophy of life,” the framework is centered around the idea that life can only be understood from within oneself, as opposed to through applying external dogmas like logic and science. Life, according to this framework, is a joyful, vibrant, and embodied experience—a philosophy now widely integrated and cherished by Germany ’s neighbor, Austria.
